paragraphs.text: A cake of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) made from Yunnan leaf in 1998 and sold under Zhong Cha Pai, the brand of the China National Tea Corporation. Its mark is the character zhong ringed in red. The label has been used on teas from several factories, so the brand does not name the factory that made this cake.

The tea was made twenty-five years after Yunnan’s state factories began [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) in 1973, which puts it in the style’s third decade. The pile was developed to produce in weeks the dark cup that Hong Kong and Guangdong drinkers knew from raw pu’er aged for years.

At twenty-eight years old it is well into what the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf goes on changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why the way a cake has been stored matters as much as its age.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
